name: COMPAT_SYSCALL_DEFINE1(sysinfo, struct compat_sysinfo __user *, info)
prose: Precondition: info is a user-space pointer to a buffer of sizeof(struct compat_sysinfo) bytes (it may be NULL or invalid; the copy is checked). Postcondition: the function gathers the current system statistics with do_sysinfo(), and if the upper 32 bits of totalram or totalswap are nonzero it shifts all memory/swap values right and doubles mem_unit until mem_unit reaches PAGE_SIZE, then zero-fills a compat_sysinfo, copies the (possibly scaled) uptime, loads, totalram, freeram, sharedram, bufferram, totalswap, freeswap, procs, totalhigh, freehigh and mem_unit into it, and returns 0, or returns -EFAULT if copy_to_user() fails (buffer contents then unspecified).
note: Read sys.c:2989-3035: do_sysinfo, scaling when the upper 32 bits of totalram or totalswap are set (mem_unit doubled until PAGE_SIZE, values shifted), zero-filled compat struct, -EFAULT on copy_to_user failure. Prose correct, kept.

name: SYSCALL_DEFINE3(getresuid, uid_t __user *, ruidp, uid_t __user *, euidp, uid_t __user *, suidp)
prose: Generated function __x64_sys_getresuid(ruidp, euidp, suidp). Precondition: ruidp, euidp and suidp are user-space pointers, which may be invalid, in which case the corresponding put_user faults. Postcondition: it returns 0 only if the current task's real, effective and saved-set user ids were all written, in that order, to ruidp, euidp and suidp; otherwise it returns the negative error code of the first failing put_user (e.g. -EFAULT) and no later value is written.
note: Read sys.c:788-805: values are converted with from_kuid_munged for the caller's user namespace, written in order with put_user, stopping at the first failure. Prose correct, kept.

name: SYSCALL_DEFINE3(getresgid, gid_t __user *, rgidp, gid_t __user *, egidp, gid_t __user *, sgidp)
prose: Generated function __x64_sys_getresgid(rgidp, egidp, sgidp). Precondition: rgidp, egidp and sgidp are user-space pointers, which may be invalid, in which case the corresponding put_user faults. Postcondition: it returns 0 only if the current task's real, effective and saved-set group ids were all written, in that order, to rgidp, egidp and sgidp; otherwise it returns the negative error code of the first failing put_user (e.g. -EFAULT) and no later value is written.
note: Read sys.c:877-: same structure as getresuid for gids. Prose correct, kept.

name: SYSCALL_DEFINE3(setresuid, uid_t, ruid, uid_t, euid, uid_t, suid)
prose: Generated function __x64_sys_setresuid(ruid, euid, suid). Precondition: none. Postcondition: it returns exactly what __sys_setresuid(ruid, euid, suid) returns — 0 on success or a negative errno such as -EINVAL, -EPERM, -ENOMEM or an LSM error — and has no effect other than that call.
note: Read sys.c:783-786: returns __sys_setresuid(...); its failure values include -EINVAL, -EPERM, -ENOMEM, errors from set_user (for example -EAGAIN), the LSM hook and set_cred_ucounts, as 'such as' in the prose already hedges. Prose kept.

name: SYSCALL_DEFINE3(setresgid, gid_t, rgid, gid_t, egid, gid_t, sgid)
prose: Generated function __x64_sys_setresgid(rgid, egid, sgid). Precondition: none. Postcondition: it returns exactly what __sys_setresgid(rgid, egid, sgid) returns — 0 on success or a negative errno such as -EINVAL, -EPERM, -ENOMEM or an LSM error — and has no effect other than that call.
note: Read sys.c:872-875: returns __sys_setresgid(...). Prose correct, kept.

name: SYSCALL_DEFINE1(setfsuid, uid_t, uid)
prose: Generated function __x64_sys_setfsuid(uid). Precondition: none. Postcondition: it returns exactly what __sys_setfsuid(uid) returns, namely the task's previous fsuid munged into its current user namespace (a non-negative uid value), whether or not the fsuid was actually changed, and has no effect other than that call.
note: Read sys.c:900-943: __sys_setfsuid returns the previous fsuid munged into the caller's namespace in every outcome (invalid uid, prepare_creds failure, no permission, no change, or committed change). Prose correct, kept.

name: SYSCALL_DEFINE1(setfsgid, gid_t, gid)
prose: Generated function __x64_sys_setfsgid(gid). Precondition: none. Postcondition: it returns exactly what __sys_setfsgid(gid) returns, namely the task's previous fsgid munged into its current user namespace (a non-negative gid value), whether or not the fsgid was actually changed, and has no effect other than that call.
note: Read sys.c:948-987: __sys_setfsgid returns the previous fsgid in every outcome. Prose correct, kept.

name: fill_stats_for_tgid
prose: Precondition: stats points to a writable struct taskstats and tgid is a pid value interpreted in the caller's active pid namespace. Postcondition: the function always writes TASKSTATS_VERSION into stats->version and always releases the RCU read lock it acquires; it returns 0 after overwriting stats with the saved statistics of the thread group's dead tasks (zeros if none) plus the accumulated statistics of every non-exiting live thread of that group, or it returns -ESRCH, leaving the rest of stats untouched, when no task with that virtual pid exists or when lock_task_sighand() on the group leader fails, and in no case does it retain a lock or a task reference.
note: Read taskstats.c:240-281. Reviewer claims: round-1 and round-2 (-ESRCH also when lock_task_sighand fails; stats untouched in that case) RIGHT and already in prose; round-15 (version not written on the -ESRCH path) is WRONG: stats->version = TASKSTATS_VERSION is written after the out label (line 275), so it is written on every return including -ESRCH. Prose kept.

name: SYSCALL_DEFINE3(setitimer, int, which, struct __kernel_old_itimerval __user *, value,
prose: Precondition: value, if non-NULL, points to a readable user-space struct __kernel_old_itimerval and ovalue, if non-NULL, points to a writable user-space struct __kernel_old_itimerval. Postcondition: it returns 0 after setting the timer selected by which from *value (or clearing that timer when value is NULL, after a one-time warning) and, when ovalue is non-NULL, storing the timer's previous setting at ovalue; it returns -EFAULT if reading *value fails or if the final store to ovalue fails (in the latter case the timer has already been changed), and it returns -EINVAL without changing any timer if which is not ITIMER_REAL, ITIMER_VIRTUAL or ITIMER_PROF or if a timeval in *value is invalid.
note: Read itimer.c:351-375: get_itimerval error returned; NULL value gives a zeroed set_buffer with a one-time warning; do_setitimer error returned; put_itimerval failure gives -EFAULT after the timer was already changed. Prose correct, kept.

name: COMPAT_SYSCALL_DEFINE3(setitimer, int, which,
prose: Precondition: value, if non-NULL, points to a readable user-space struct old_itimerval32 and ovalue, if non-NULL, points to a writable user-space struct old_itimerval32. Postcondition: it returns 0 after setting the timer selected by which from *value (or clearing that timer when value is NULL, after a one-time warning) and, when ovalue is non-NULL, storing the timer's previous setting at ovalue; it returns -EFAULT if reading *value fails or if the final store to ovalue fails (in the latter case the timer has already been changed), and it returns -EINVAL without changing any timer if which is not ITIMER_REAL, ITIMER_VIRTUAL or ITIMER_PROF or if a timeval in *value is invalid.
note: Read itimer.c:378-421 (CONFIG_COMPAT or CONFIG_ALPHA): same with get_old_itimerval32 (-EFAULT or -EINVAL for invalid timevals) and put_old_itimerval32. Prose correct, kept.

name: __run_posix_cpu_timers
prose: Runs the expired POSIX CPU timers of the current task tsk; called from run_posix_cpu_timers (posix-cpu-timers.c:1465-1495) with interrupts disabled after the fast path found expired timers, and only if tsk is not exiting and no CPU-timer task work is already scheduled. There are two definitions. With CONFIG_POSIX_CPU_TIMERS_TASK_WORK (line 1279) it does not run the timers itself: if tsk->posix_cputimers_work.scheduled is already set it only issues WARN_ON_ONCE and returns, otherwise it sets scheduled and queues the work with task_work_add(TWA_RESUME). Otherwise (line 1327) it calls handle_posix_cpu_timers(tsk) between lockdep_posixtimer_enter() and lockdep_posixtimer_exit(). handle_posix_cpu_timers returns immediately if lock_task_sighand fails; otherwise it collects expired thread and process timers onto a local list under the sighand lock (repeating while posix_cpu_timers_enable_work asks for it), releases the sighand lock, and then for each collected timer takes timer->it_lock, removes it from the list, reads and clears it.cpu.firing, calls cpu_timer_fire only if firing was still set (a rearm or delete race skips the event), clears it.cpu.handling and releases it_lock. No lock is held on return.
note: Packet slice contained both variants of __run_posix_cpu_timers (1279 task-work variant and 1327 direct variant); the old prose described only the direct variant and its precondition about deferred work. Read posix-cpu-timers.c:1279-1495. Reviewer claims: round-1 (runs in timer interrupt context, not task work) RIGHT for the direct variant, wrong for the task-work variant, now both stated; round-2 (firing skipped after a rearm/delete race) RIGHT and kept.

name: SYSCALL_DEFINE1(timer_delete, timer_t, timer_id)
prose: Precondition: the caller passes a POSIX timer ID and holds no locks or references on the timer. Postcondition: if timer_id identifies an existing timer, that timer is invalidated, removed from the hash and freed so its ID can be reused, and 0 is returned; if the lookup fails, -EINVAL is returned and no timer is modified; in both cases the temporary reference taken by the lookup is released and the caller retains no locks or references.
note: Read posix-timers.c:1061-1072: the scoped lookup fails with -EINVAL when the id is unknown; otherwise the timer is deleted (posix_timer_delete, which may wait for a running callback with it_lock dropped) and then unhashed and freed; returns 0. Prose correct, kept.

name: SYSCALL_DEFINE2(clock_adjtime, const clockid_t, which_clock,
prose: Precondition: utx points to user memory of at least sizeof(struct __kernel_timex) bytes that is readable and writable, and the caller holds no locks. Postcondition: -EFAULT is returned if the timex struct cannot be copied from utx, or if the clock-specific adjustment returned a non-negative value but the adjusted struct could not be copied back to utx; -EINVAL is returned if which_clock is not a valid clock; -EOPNOTSUPP is returned if the clock has no adjust callback; otherwise the return value of the clock-specific adjuster is returned, and when that value is non-negative the adjusted timex has been stored at utx; no locks or references are held on return.
note: Read posix-timers.c:1166-1181: -EFAULT if the copy in fails; do_clock_adjtime result (negative errors such as -EINVAL for an invalid clock, -EOPNOTSUPP without an adjust callback); copy back only when the result is non-negative, failing with -EFAULT. Prose correct, kept.

name: SYSCALL_DEFINE3(timer_create, const clockid_t, which_clock,
prose: Generated system call entry for timer_create(which_clock, timer_event_spec, created_timer_id) defined at posix-timers.c:574-586. If timer_event_spec is non-NULL it copies a sigevent from user space (-EFAULT on failure) and calls do_timer_create(which_clock, &event, created_timer_id), otherwise with NULL. do_timer_create (466-572) returns -EINVAL if the clock id has no k_clock, -EOPNOTSUPP if the clock has no timer_create method, -EFAULT or -EINVAL when restoring ids (timer_create_restore_ids set) if the requested id cannot be read or exceeds INT_MAX, -EAGAIN if the timer cannot be allocated, the negative error from posix_timer_add, -EINVAL if the sigevent does not name a valid target (good_sigevent), -EFAULT if storing the new id at created_timer_id fails, and the error of the clock specific timer_create callback. On success it publishes the timer on the process posix_timers list under the locks and returns 0 (the id has been stored at created_timer_id). Failure after the id has been allocated unhashes and frees the timer; the id may already have been stored at created_timer_id before a later failure (the store happens before the clock timer_create callback). No lock is held on return.
note: Macro-generated syscall wrapper (packet name __x64_sys_timer_create), named by the SYSCALL_DEFINE3 head per rule 5. Read posix-timers.c:466-600. Old prose said no timer id is published on failure; wrong in that copy_to_user of the id happens at 533 before kc->timer_create at 544; also added -EOPNOTSUPP, -EAGAIN and the restore-id errors.

name: COMPAT_SYSCALL_DEFINE3(timer_create, clockid_t, which_clock,
prose: Generated compat system call entry for timer_create(which_clock, timer_event_spec, created_timer_id) defined at posix-timers.c:589-601. If timer_event_spec is non-NULL it converts a compat sigevent with get_compat_sigevent (-EFAULT on failure) and calls do_timer_create(which_clock, &event, created_timer_id), otherwise with NULL. do_timer_create returns -EINVAL if the clock id has no k_clock, -EOPNOTSUPP if the clock has no timer_create method, -EFAULT or -EINVAL for the restore-id case, -EAGAIN if allocation fails, the error from posix_timer_add, -EINVAL if the sigevent does not name a valid target, -EFAULT if storing the new id fails, or the error of the clock specific timer_create callback; on success it publishes the timer and returns 0. The new id may already have been stored at created_timer_id when a later step fails. No lock is held on return.
note: Macro-generated compat wrapper named by the COMPAT_SYSCALL_DEFINE3 head per rule 5. Same corrections as the native timer_create (posix-timers.c:466-572).

name: SYSCALL_DEFINE2(timer_gettime, timer_t, timer_id,
prose: Generated function __x64_sys_timer_gettime(timer_id, setting). Precondition: setting points to writable user memory of at least sizeof(struct __kernel_itimerspec) bytes. Postcondition: returns 0 with the timer's interval and remaining time copied out to setting (fields the timer does not report are zero), returns -EINVAL if timer_id is outside the positive int range or does not identify a live POSIX timer of the calling process (nothing is written to setting), or returns -EFAULT if the copy out to setting fails; no locks or references are held on return.
note: Read posix-timers.c:752-763: do_timer_gettime error (-EINVAL for an invalid or dead timer) returned without writing; put_itimerspec64 failure gives -EFAULT. Prose correct, kept.

name: SYSCALL_DEFINE1(timer_getoverrun, timer_t, timer_id)
prose: Generated function timer_getoverrun(timer_id): precondition: none; timer_id may be any value. Postcondition: the function returns -EINVAL if timer_id does not identify a valid POSIX timer; otherwise it returns the cached overrun count of the last delivered signal for that timer, which is 0 when no signal has been delivered or the timer has been reset, and otherwise lies in 1..INT_MAX; no locks, references or memory are acquired or lost by the caller.
note: Read posix-timers.c:800-803 and 290-296: the lookup fails with -EINVAL for an unknown timer; otherwise it returns it_overrun_last clamped to INT_MAX (0 if no signal delivered or the timer was reset). Prose correct, kept.

name: common_timer_set
prose: Precondition: timr points to a valid k_itimer and new_setting points to a valid itimerspec64, and old_setting may be NULL. Postcondition: if old_setting is non-NULL, *old_setting is filled from the timer's current state via common_timer_get before any cancellation attempt; then if kc->timer_try_to_cancel(timr) returns less than zero the function returns TIMER_RETRY with the timer otherwise unchanged; otherwise it sets it_status to POSIX_TIMER_DISARMED, sets it_interval to new_setting->it_interval converted to ktime when new_setting->it_value is nonzero or to 0 when it_value is zero, resets it_overrun_last to 0 and it_overrun to -1, and if new_setting->it_value is zero returns 0 with the timer disarmed; otherwise it computes expires from new_setting->it_value, converts it to the host time namespace when flags has TIMER_ABSTIME, calls kc->timer_arm(timr, expires, flags & TIMER_ABSTIME, timr->it_sigev_notify == SIGEV_NONE), sets it_status to POSIX_TIMER_ARMED unless sigev_notify is SIGEV_NONE (in which case it remains POSIX_TIMER_DISARMED), and returns 0; no locks, references or memory are acquired or lost by the caller.
note: Read posix-timers.c:872-919: old_setting is filled first (also when TIMER_RETRY follows); timer_try_to_cancel < 0 returns TIMER_RETRY; posix_timer_set_common sets it_interval (0 when it_value is zero) and resets overrun accounting; zero it_value returns 0 disarmed; else timer_arm is called and the status becomes ARMED unless SIGEV_NONE. Prose correct, kept; both reviewer claims already reflected.

name: __tick_broadcast_oneshot_control
prose: Handles entry to or exit from a deep idle state for the current CPU with respect to the broadcast timer (tick-broadcast.c:971-987); state is TICK_BROADCAST_ENTER or TICK_BROADCAST_EXIT. It first calls tick_oneshot_wakeup_control(state, td, cpu): if that returns 0 the function returns 0 at once. If it returns a non-zero value (the prose of earlier rounds called it -EINVAL or -ENODEV) that value is not returned; the function continues: if tick_broadcast_device.evtdev is non-NULL it returns the result of ___tick_broadcast_oneshot_control(state, td, cpu), otherwise it returns -EBUSY. It takes no locks itself.
note: Read tick-broadcast.c:971-987. Reviewer round-1 claim (only 0 or -EBUSY possible; wakeup errors swallowed) is partly RIGHT: the helper's non-zero value is ignored, but the return value of ___tick_broadcast_oneshot_control is not shown in this slice, so 'only 0 and -EBUSY' was removed from the prose. The old sentence that 0 is returned even when the helper's error is swallowed was wrong: after a non-zero helper result the function goes on to the broadcast path (979-986).

name: SYSCALL_DEFINE1(time32, old_time32_t __user *, tloc)
prose: Precondition: tloc, if non-NULL, is a writable user address. Postcondition: returns the current real time in seconds truncated to old_time32_t, storing that value to tloc when tloc is non-NULL, and returns -EFAULT if that store fails.
note: Read time.c:105-117: returns the seconds truncated to old_time32_t; -EFAULT if the optional put_user fails; force_successful_syscall_return marks a negative-looking value as success. Prose correct, kept.

name: SYSCALL_DEFINE1(stime32, old_time32_t __user *, tptr)
prose: Precondition: tptr is a readable user address holding a 32-bit seconds value. Postcondition: reads the seconds into a timespec64 with tv_nsec zero, runs security_settime64 and, if it succeeds, sets the clock with do_settimeofday64 and returns 0; returns -EFAULT if the user read fails or the security check's error code if it fails.
note: Read time.c:119-135: -EFAULT if get_user fails; the error of security_settime64; otherwise do_settimeofday64 (whose result is ignored) and 0. Prose correct, kept.

name: ftrace_find_rec_direct
prose: Precondition: ip is any unsigned long and direct_functions is a valid RCU-protected hash; the function disables preemption around the lookup. Postcondition: if direct_functions contains an entry for ip, the function returns that entry's direct value; otherwise it returns 0. Preemption is restored before every return, and no lock, reference, or memory is retained.
note: Read ftrace.c:2602-2612: guard(preempt_notrace) around __ftrace_lookup_ip on rcu_dereference_sched(direct_functions); returns entry->direct or 0. Prose correct, kept.

name: add_next_hash
prose: Computes the filter and notrace hashes that result from adding the sub-ops hash subops_hash to the ops hash ops_hash (ftrace.c:3440-3507); *filter_hash and *notrace_hash are outputs whose incoming values are not read. If either ops_hash->filter_hash or subops_hash->filter_hash is empty, *filter_hash is set to EMPTY_HASH. Otherwise (with a WARN_ON_ONCE if ops_hash->notrace_hash is non-empty) it allocates and fills *filter_hash with a copy of subops_hash->filter_hash (-ENOMEM with *filter_hash NULL on failure), removes the entries of subops_hash->notrace_hash from that copy only, then appends the entries of ops_hash->filter_hash with append_hash; if that fails it frees *filter_hash, sets it to EMPTY_HASH and returns the error. So the ops filter entries are added without removing subops notrace entries. If the resulting *filter_hash is empty it allocates *notrace_hash (-ENOMEM with *notrace_hash NULL on failure, *filter_hash unchanged) and fills it with the intersection of ops_hash->notrace_hash and subops_hash->notrace_hash using intersect_hash (EMPTY_HASH if either input is empty or the intersection is empty; on an error it frees *notrace_hash, sets it to EMPTY_HASH and returns the error). If *filter_hash is non-empty *notrace_hash is left untouched. Returns 0 on success and a negative errno on failure; hashes allocated on success are owned by the caller.
note: Read ftrace.c:3315-3345 (intersect_hash) and 3440-3507. Reviewer claims: round-1 (allocation failure leaves NULL, not EMPTY_HASH) RIGHT and in the new prose; round-2 (WARN_ON_ONCE only in the non-empty filter branch) RIGHT; round-15 (subops notrace entries are removed only from the copied subops filter before appending the ops filter, not from the whole union) RIGHT (3462-3469); the old first sentence about the union was wrong and is corrected.

name: ftrace_profile_init_cpu
prose: Precondition: cpu is a valid per-CPU index for ftrace_profile_stats. Postcondition: returns 0 after resetting an already-created stat (hash non-NULL) or after successfully allocating a fresh hash table and preallocating the profile pages; returns -ENOMEM (-12) if the hash allocation fails or if the page preallocation fails, in which case the partially allocated hash is freed and set to NULL and no memory is leaked.
note: Read ftrace.c:672-704: reset path returns 0; kcalloc failure -ENOMEM; ftrace_profile_pages_init failure frees the hash, sets it to NULL and returns -ENOMEM. Prose correct, kept; the old contract was rejected only by mechanical checks and the function mutates per-CPU global state (rule 4), so it was dropped.

name: ftrace_profile_init
prose: Precondition: none. Postcondition: returns 0 if every possible CPU's profile stat was initialized successfully; otherwise returns -ENOMEM (-12), the error code returned by ftrace_profile_init_cpu for the first CPU whose initialization failed, and the remaining CPUs are skipped.
note: Read ftrace.c:706-718: loops for_each_possible_cpu and stops at the first non-zero ftrace_profile_init_cpu result (-ENOMEM), returning it. Prose correct, kept; old contract dropped (rule 4).

name: ring_buffer_map
prose: Precondition: cpu must be a cpu number present in buffer->cpumask (otherwise -EINVAL is returned with no state changed) and vma must be a valid vm_area_struct. Postcondition: the function holds cpu_buffer->mapping_lock from after the cpumask check until it returns; if cpu_buffer->user_mapped is nonzero it calls __rb_map_vma and, only if that returns 0, calls __rb_inc_dec_mapped(cpu_buffer, true), returning 0 on success or the negative errno from either call (-EPERM, -EINVAL or -ENOMEM from __rb_map_vma, or -EOPNOTSUPP from its non-MMU version, -EINVAL or -EBUSY from __rb_inc_dec_mapped), with the mapping counters unchanged in those failure cases but the vma left populated and its flags modified if __rb_map_vma had succeeded; if cpu_buffer->user_mapped is zero it takes buffer->mutex (held until return), allocates the meta page (returning that error unchanged on failure), allocates the subbuf id array (on failure freeing the meta page and returning -ENOMEM), increments cpu_buffer->resize_disabled, takes cpu_buffer->reader_lock to install the meta page contents and subbuf id table, releases reader_lock, then calls __rb_map_vma, and if that succeeds takes reader_lock again to increment cpu_buffer->mapped and set cpu_buffer->user_mapped to 1 and returns 0 leaving resize_disabled incremented and the meta page and subbuf id table installed, while if __rb_map_vma fails it frees the subbuf id table and sets cpu_buffer->subbuf_ids to NULL, frees the meta page, decrements resize_disabled, and returns the error from __rb_map_vma with the vma possibly partially populated and its flags modified.
note: Read ring_buffer.c:7393-7455 and __rb_map_vma (7300-7390, -EOPNOTSUPP at 7389). Reviewer claims: round-1 (failure after __rb_map_vma success leaves the vma mapped) RIGHT and in prose; round-15 (error list omits -EOPNOTSUPP) RIGHT; added.

name: ltl_atoms_init
prose: Precondition: mon is the LTL monitor associated with task. Postcondition: the void function always sets LTL_SLEEP, LTL_WAKE, LTL_ABORT_SLEEP, LTL_WOKEN_BY_HARDIRQ, LTL_WOKEN_BY_NMI and LTL_WOKEN_BY_EQUAL_OR_HIGHER_PRIO to false; when task_creation is true it additionally sets LTL_KTHREAD_SHOULD_STOP, LTL_NANOSLEEP_CLOCK_MONOTONIC, LTL_NANOSLEEP_CLOCK_TAI, LTL_NANOSLEEP_TIMER_ABSTIME, LTL_CLOCK_NANOSLEEP, LTL_FUTEX_WAIT, LTL_FUTEX_LOCK_PI and LTL_BLOCK_ON_RT_MUTEX to false; if task->flags has PF_KTHREAD it sets LTL_KERNEL_THREAD to true, sets LTL_FUTEX_WAIT, LTL_FUTEX_LOCK_PI, LTL_NANOSLEEP_CLOCK_MONOTONIC, LTL_NANOSLEEP_CLOCK_TAI, LTL_NANOSLEEP_TIMER_ABSTIME and LTL_CLOCK_NANOSLEEP to false, sets LTL_TASK_IS_MIGRATION to true exactly when task->comm starts with "migration/" and false otherwise, sets LTL_TASK_IS_RCU to true exactly when task->comm starts with "rcu" and false otherwise, and leaves LTL_KTHREAD_SHOULD_STOP unchanged (except for the task_creation assignment above); otherwise (no PF_KTHREAD) it sets LTL_KTHREAD_SHOULD_STOP, LTL_KERNEL_THREAD, LTL_TASK_IS_RCU and LTL_TASK_IS_MIGRATION to false; LTL_BLOCK_ON_RT_MUTEX is modified only when task_creation is true (set to false at line 53).
note: Read sleep.c:36-83. Reviewer claims round-2 and round-15 (task_creation also sets LTL_BLOCK_ON_RT_MUTEX to false, so 'never modified' is wrong) are RIGHT; corrected in both places.

name: trace_user_fault_buffer_enable
prose: Precondition: none; the function takes trace_user_buffer_mutex via guard and releases it on every return path. Postcondition: it returns 0 either when the global trace_user_buffer already exists (incrementing its refcount) or when a new info structure, its per-CPU array, and a TRACE_MARKER_MAX_SIZE buffer for every possible CPU are allocated and installed as the global trace_user_buffer with ref 1; it returns -ENOMEM (-12) if kmalloc of the info structure, alloc_percpu, or any per-CPU kmalloc_node fails, freeing all partially allocated state and leaving the global trace_user_buffer unchanged.
note: Read trace.c:7267-7310: guard(mutex) on trace_user_buffer_mutex; existing buffer gives 0 (refcount incremented, line 7276); -ENOMEM for kmalloc, alloc_percpu or any per-CPU kmalloc_node failure with the partial state freed. Prose correct, kept; old contract dropped (the function mutates a global, rule 4).

name: tracing_buffers_read
prose: Precondition: filp is an open tracing-buffer file whose private_data is a valid ftrace_buffer_info with an initialized iterator, ubuf points to a user buffer writable for at least count bytes, and info->read is not larger than the size of the spare page info->spare. Postcondition: it returns 0 when count is 0, when ring_buffer_read_page fails while the trace is non-empty or the iterator is closed, or when ring_buffer_read_page fails on an empty open trace and update_last_data_if_empty succeeds; it returns -EBUSY for a snapshot iterator whose trace's current tracer uses max_tr; it returns the negative errno of a failed ring_buffer_alloc_read_page or of a failed wait_on_pipe; it returns -EAGAIN when the trace is empty, not closed and O_NONBLOCK is set; it returns -EFAULT without advancing *ppos or info->read when copy_to_user copies no bytes; otherwise it returns the positive number of bytes copied and advances *ppos and info->read by that amount, and transferring no memory or reference to the caller (the code shown takes no lock).
note: Slice cut the head (name outside slice); real function tracing_buffers_read at trace.c:8439-8514 read in full. Reviewer round-15 claim (count 0 yields -EFAULT) is WRONG: the function returns 0 for count == 0 at lines 8449-8450 before any copy. The old claim that a trace access lock is taken is not supported by the code shown and was removed.

name: rb_simple_write
prose: Precondition: filp->private_data points to a valid trace_array (tr) and ubuf is a user-space buffer readable for cnt bytes. Postcondition: if kstrtoul_from_user fails to parse the value it returns that negative error code without incrementing *ppos and without taking any lock; otherwise, when tr->array_buffer.buffer is non-NULL it takes trace_types_lock (released before return) and, if the parsed value differs from tracer_tracing_is_on(tr), turns tracing on (calling tr->current_trace->start if set) or off (calling tr->current_trace->stop if set and waking ring buffer waiters on all CPUs), while if the buffer is NULL nothing is toggled and no lock is taken; when the buffer is non-NULL the lock is taken before the comparison, so it is held (and released) even when the value already matches the current state and nothing is toggled; in every non-parse-failure case *ppos is incremented by one and cnt is returned.
note: Read trace.c:9677-9709. Reviewer claims all RIGHT: round-1 (buffer NULL path still updates ppos and returns cnt), round-2 and round-15 (the mutex is taken whenever the buffer is non-NULL, before the match check at 9690-9691); prose corrected.

name: parse_pred
prose: Precondition: str points to a NUL-terminated filter expression, data is the trace_event_call whose fields are looked up, pos is the base offset used for error positions, pe is a valid parse-error record, and *pred_ptr is writable. Postcondition: on success it returns the number of characters consumed and stores the fully initialised predicate in *pred_ptr; otherwise it returns -1 when no field name is present at the current position, -ENOMEM when an allocation fails, or -EINVAL after recording a parse error in pe, and in every failure case it frees any predicate allocated so far and leaves *pred_ptr untouched.
note: Slice cut the head (name outside slice); real function parse_pred at trace_events_filter.c:1634-2095 read at both ends. Reviewer round-15 claim (the no-field case returns -EINVAL after parse_error, not -1) is WRONG: when no identifier is present the function returns -1 at line 1667-1668 with no parse_error; an unknown field name returns -EINVAL after FILT_ERR_FIELD_NOT_FOUND (1678-1680), and every other parse error goes through err_free (-EINVAL) or err_mem (-ENOMEM) after freeing the predicate (2089-2094). *pred_ptr is only written on success (2086-2087). Prose kept.

name: __synth_event_add_val
prose: Precondition: trace_state refers to a trace opened by synth_event_trace_start; when field_name is non-NULL, add_next mode has not been used; when field_name is NULL, add_name mode has not been used and fewer values have been added than the event has fields; val is the value to write, or for a non-dynamic string field a non-NULL pointer to a string. Postcondition: returns 0 after writing the field (or without writing anything if the trace is disabled); returns -EINVAL when trace_state is NULL, the two add modes are mixed, the next-field index is past the last field, the field is a dynamic string, the string pointer is NULL, or (only when the event has no fields) field_name matches no field; when field_name matches no field but the event has at least one field, the last field is used instead (the string-field checks that follow can still return -EINVAL for it); the add_name/add_next flag is set when the mode check passes (even if the trace is disabled), and in next-field mode cur_field is incremented before any later error.
note: Read trace_events_synth.c:1981-2069. Reviewer claims: round-1 (state changes before an error) RIGHT and in prose; round-2 (an unmatched name leaves the last field, not NULL: field is only NULL when the event has no fields) RIGHT and in prose; round-15 (the last-field case can still return -EINVAL for a dynamic or NULL string, 2036-2044) RIGHT; prose corrected. Note my reading tool hid the lines setting add_name/add_next (2000, 2006); verified with a raw read.

name: kprobe_trace_self_tests_init
prose: Precondition: called once at late_initcall after the tracing subsystem is initialized. Postcondition: returns -ENODEV if tracing is disabled; returns 0 without running any test if tracing selftests are disabled; otherwise it creates, enables and checks two test probes (each expected to record exactly one hit), disables and deletes them, waits for the kprobe optimizer to finish, prints an OK or failure message, and returns 0 even when individual test steps fail.
note: Read trace_kprobe.c:2075-2194: -ENODEV when tracing_is_disabled (2082-2083); 0 when tracing_selftest_disabled (2085-2086); otherwise runs the checks, counts failures in warn, prints OK or NG and returns 0 (2128-2129, 2189-2193). Prose correct, kept; old contract dropped (the function creates and deletes global probes, rule 4).

name: run_osnoise
prose: Precondition: the per-CPU osnoise variables returned by this_cpu_osn_var() are initialized, the osnoise tracer options and data (osnoise_options, osnoise_data, tracing_thresh) are set, and the function is called from the osnoise sampling kthread with preemption and interrupts enabled unless the OSN_IRQ_DISABLE/OSN_PREEMPT_DISABLE options request otherwise. Postcondition: the function returns 0 after the sampling loop ends (by runtime expiry, kthread_should_stop(), or the total-overflow taint break), having cleared osn_var->sampling, restored any preemption/IRQ state it disabled, saved and recorded the sample, notified a new maximum latency, and possibly stopped tracing; it returns -1 only when a negative noise value is detected, in which case it taints the tracer and returns immediately without clearing osn_var->sampling, without restoring preemption/IRQ state, and without recording the sample.
note: Read trace_osnoise.c:1405-1600. Reviewer round-15 claim (the negative-noise 'goto out' reaches the cleanup point) is WRONG: the out: label sits after the final 'return 0;' and only returns ret (1598-1599), so a negative noise value returns without clearing osn_var->sampling, without re-enabling IRQs or preemption and without recording the sample, exactly as the prose says. The total-overflow taint only breaks the loop and the normal tail runs (1498-1501, 1560-1597). Prose kept.

name: __lockup_detector_reconfigure
prose: In the CONFIG_SOFTLOCKUP_DETECTOR build the caller holds watchdog_mutex, while in the !CONFIG_SOFTLOCKUP_DETECTOR build the function is called without watchdog_mutex. The function acquires cpus_read_lock, stops the hard lockup detector, optionally sets watchdog_thresh to READ_ONCE(watchdog_thresh_next) when thresh_changed is true, calls lockup_detector_update_enable(), restarts the hard lockup detector, and releases cpus_read_lock before returning no value; in the CONFIG_SOFTLOCKUP_DETECTOR build it also calls softlockup_stop_all() (which stops the softlockup detectors on CPUs in watchdog_allowed_mask and clears watchdog_allowed_mask only when softlockup_initialized is true, and otherwise does nothing), calls set_sample_period(), and, only when watchdog_enabled && watchdog_thresh, calls softlockup_start_all() to copy watchdog_cpumask into watchdog_allowed_mask and start a softlockup detector on each CPU in that mask, leaving watchdog_allowed_mask as softlockup_stop_all() left it when that condition is false.
note: Read watchdog.c:945-966 (CONFIG_SOFTLOCKUP_DETECTOR) and 997-1006 (otherwise), and softlockup_stop_all (903-914: returns at once if softlockup_initialized is false, else stops the detectors on watchdog_allowed_mask CPUs and clears the mask). Both reviewer claims (precondition about watchdog_mutex differs per build; stop_all returns early when not initialized) are already reflected. Prose kept.

name: sw842_debugfs_create
prose: Precondition: none. Postcondition: if the debugfs subsystem has not been initialized it creates nothing and returns -19 (-ENODEV); otherwise it creates the sw842 debugfs directory plus the template-count files (ignoring any failure of those creations) and returns 0, leaving the created debugfs entries for sw842_debugfs_remove to delete.
note: Read lib/842/842_debugfs.h:16-43: -ENODEV when debugfs is not initialised, else creates the directory and the atomic_t files (their results are not checked) and returns 0. Prose correct, kept; old contract dropped (the function creates global debugfs entries, rule 4).

name: vm_module_tags_populate
prose: Precondition: module_tags.start_addr, module_tags.size, vm_module_tags->nr_pages and vm_module_tags->pages describe the module-tags vmalloc area, module_tags.size may extend beyond the currently populated end, and vm_module_tags->pages has room for the additional page pointers. Postcondition: if the mapping already covers module_tags.start_addr + module_tags.size, no pages are allocated and result is 0 after KASAN-unpoisoning that range; otherwise on success all pages needed to cover the new end are allocated and mapped, vm_module_tags->nr_pages is increased by the number mapped, KASAN shadow is allocated for any newly needed shadow range, the whole range from module_tags.start_addr to the new end is KASAN-unpoisoned, and result is 0, while on failure result is -ENOMEM, the nr allocated pages are released, vm_module_tags->nr_pages is unchanged, no KASAN shadow is allocated and no KASAN-unpoisoning is done, and this function does nothing to undo a partial mapping that vmap_pages_range may have made before failing; the failure test covers both a shortfall in the allocated page count and a negative vmap_pages_range result.
note: Read alloc_tag.c:432-491. Reviewer round-15 claim (the failure path releases the allocated pages, so partially mapped pages cannot be said to remain mapped) is RIGHT in that the code calls release_pages(arg, nr) at 463 and says nothing about a partial mapping; the old claim that the mapping 'may extend beyond its previous extent' is not supported by any line and was replaced. Round-2 claim is likewise unsupported by this function.

name: assoc_array_insert_into_terminal_node
prose: Precondition: edit is an insertion edit whose tree walk terminated at the terminal node node at the given level, with edit->segment_cache[ASSOC_ARRAY_FAN_OUT] already holding the new leaf's segment, and the ops callbacks (compare_object, get_object_key_chunk, diff_objects, get_key_chunk) are usable on the leaves stored in node and on index_key. Postcondition: the tree itself is left unmodified and the function returns true after recording in edit exactly one pending update for the caller to apply - a replacement (edit->leaf_p and edit->dead_leaf), a plain insertion into a free slot (edit->leaf_p and edit->adjust_count_on), or a node split / shortcut-plus-split (edit->set[0], edit->set_backpointers, edit->excised_meta, edit->leaf_p, edit->adjust_count_on and the newly allocated nodes and optional shortcut in edit->new_meta) - and it returns false only when kzalloc of new_n0, new_n1 or new_s0 fails, in which case the tree is still unmodified and every node or shortcut allocated before the failure is recorded in edit->new_meta so the caller can free it.
note: Packet name matches the real static function at lib/assoc_array.c:475 (slice began inside it). Returns verified: true at the replace/insert-free-slot/split paths (518, 530, 712) and false only after a failed kzalloc of new_n0, new_n1 or new_s0 (542, 546, 747). Prose correct, kept.
